609	\section{Exploratory Extension to Relation Extraction}\label{app:re_extension}
610	
611	We extend the NER evaluation to relation extraction (RE) on SciERC as an exploratory single-benchmark analysis.
612	RE produces sets of (head, relation, tail) triples with partial overlap; 40\% of RE instances receive zero F1, and entity span errors account for 55.5\% of RE false negatives---a prerequisite failure that consistency signals cannot detect (\S\ref{app:additional}).
613	All RE results use Qwen3-8B unless noted; single-seed ($\text{seed}{=}42$) for $N{=}8$ analyses, 3-seed for $N{=}16$.
614	
615	\paragraph{Quality estimation.}
616	RE quality estimation is reported in Table~\ref{tab:multiseed} (3-seed means).
617	The signal ranking differs from NER: VC leads ($\rho{=}0.309{\pm}0.024$), but LP rises to \#2 ($\rho{=}0.297{\pm}0.022$), above FK, SJ, and EM---a reversal reflecting RE's higher sensitivity to per-sample scoring.
618	RE miscalibration is more severe than NER (ECE 0.109--0.339; Figure~\ref{fig:reliability}).
619	
620	\paragraph{Selection.}
621	Table~\ref{tab:re_cond_selection} presents RE selection at $N{=}8$: no signal outperforms single-sample (0.404) on the full set ($n{=}397$) or the non-zero subset ($n{=}238$), with 18.1~pp of unrealized oracle headroom.
622	At $N{=}16$ (Qwen3-4B, Table~\ref{tab:re_n16_selection}), LP is the sole positive signal ($\Delta{=}{+}0.7$~pp, $p{=}0.058$), consistent with LP being the strongest RE selection signal across scales.
623	
624	\paragraph{Scale ablation.}
625	At 4B scale (Qwen3-4B, $N{=}8$, $\text{seed}{=}42$), RE quality estimation shows FK $\rho{=}0.359$ and LP $\rho{=}0.351$, both above their 8B counterparts (FK 0.275, LP 0.266), while SJ declines ($0.267$ vs.\ $0.250$).
626	Selection remains below single-sample on RE ($\Delta$ up to $-3.4$~pp) despite 17.1~pp of oracle headroom.
627	
628	\paragraph{Free-form decoding.}
629	RE LP selection consistently reverses direction under free-form decoding ($+1.8{\pm}0.1$~pp across 4 seeds vs.\ $-0.9$~pp under constrained decoding at 8B; \S\ref{app:freeform_ablation}), suggesting constrained decoding's fixed template obscures LP signal in RE (\S\ref{app:mbr_discussion}).

691	\section{MBR Decoding and Task-Specific Interactions}\label{app:mbr_discussion}
692	
693	\paragraph{Connection to MBR decoding.}
694	Our selection strategies instantiate minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, muller2021understanding}: each selects $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} U(y_i, y_j)$ with utility $U$ defined by SJ, EM, or entity overlap.
695	Despite MBR's success in machine translation \cite{freitag2022high} and its extension to summarization, code generation, and captioning \cite{jinnai2024mbr}, all variants fail here: despite positive within-instance utility--F1 correlation, selection gains are limited by instance degeneracy---the core of the correlation-selection gap.
696	\citet{eikema2025structured} study structure-conditional MBR decoding and find that standard utility functions degrade on structured outputs---consistent with our finding that consensus-proximity selection fails in IE despite its success in machine translation.
697	
698	\paragraph{Task-specific decoding interactions.}
699	The free-form ablation reveals divergent behavior across tasks.
700	On RE, LP selection flips from $-0.68$~pp (constrained) to $+1.69$~pp (free-form; preliminary, single RE benchmark), a reversal that spans all 7 relation types and is driven by selective variance reallocation ($p{<}0.0001$).
701	The win/loss ratio shifts from 36:59 (constrained) to 45:45 (free-form), with the gains concentrated on relation-dense instances (mean 3.3 gold relations).
702	This interaction does not generalize to NER, where selection remains negligible under both regimes.
703	This ablation uses a single seed (seed${=}42$); whether the RE reversal replicates across seeds and generalizes to other RE benchmarks warrants further investigation.
704	The non-tied subset ($n{=}210$) is partially reshuffled under free-form decoding: Jaccard similarity between the constrained and free-form non-tied sets is 0.472, indicating that 87 instances newly gain LP discrimination while others lose it, yielding a $3{\times}$ increase in within-instance LP range for the newly non-tied subset.
705	Despite this reshuffling, aggregate NER selection gains remain negligible---score compression is not a fixed property of specific instances but rather a pervasive regime that shifts across instances without producing net selection improvement.
706	Free-form decoding also slightly improves quality estimation (NER VC $\rho$: 0.379$\to$0.409), though this does not translate to selection gains.
707

806	
807	\paragraph{Instance complexity drives failure.}
808	Table~\ref{tab:stable_failures} stratifies instances by failure stability.
809	Stable failures (all 3 seeds) involve more gold relations (2.12 vs.\ 1.62 for never-fail instances) and higher single-sample F1 (0.688 vs.\ 0.429), indicating that LP mis-selects on instances where the model already performs well---precisely the instances where selection would be most valuable.

We analyze RE LP selection failures across three random seeds (constrained decoding, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$, Qwen3-8B) to assess whether failures are systematic or stochastic.

\paragraph{Pairwise overlap.}
LP selection failures (instances where LP-selected F1 $<$ single-sample F1) show moderate cross-seed stability: the average pairwise Jaccard similarity is 0.42 (range: 0.38--0.46), indicating that failures are partially systematic---driven by instance complexity---but not fully deterministic.
The 3-way intersection contains 34 instances (27.9\% of any-seed failures), confirming a stable failure core.

\paragraph{Instance complexity drives failure.}
Table~\ref{tab:stable_failures} stratifies instances by failure stability.
Stable failures (all 3 seeds) involve more gold relations (2.12 vs.\ 1.62 for never-fail instances) and higher single-sample F1 (0.688 vs.\ 0.429), indicating that LP mis-selects on instances where the model already performs well---precisely the instances where selection would be most valuable.
Failure rate increases monotonically with gold relation count: 4.3\% at 1 relation, 20.7\% at 3 relations, 26.2\% at 6 relations.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{RE LP selection failure stability across 3 seeds (SciERC, $N{=}8$). Stable failures concentrate on relation-dense instances with high single-sample F1.}
\label{tab:stable_failures}
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
Group & $n$ & Gold rels & Greedy F1 & LP $\Delta$F1 \\
\midrule
Stable fail (3 seeds) & 34 & 2.12 & 0.688 & $-$0.499 \\
Fail 2+ seeds & 26 & 2.46 & 0.774 & $-$0.450 \\
Fail 1 seed & 62 & 2.32 & 0.692 & $-$0.239 \\
Never fail & 429 & 1.62 & 0.429 & $+$0.041 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Flip instances.}
Only 5 RE instances with gold relations flip from LP failure (constrained) to LP success (free-form), with mean gold relation count 3.67 (well above the population mean of 1.86).
These instances show large constrained LP errors ($\Delta{=}{-}0.430$) that reverse under free-form decoding ($\Delta{=}{+}0.503$), but their rarity (5/397) confirms that the RE selection flip is driven by aggregate variance reallocation rather than systematic instance-level correction.

\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Self-consistency and test-time scaling.}
Self-consistency \cite{wang2023selfconsistency} improves reasoning via majority voting; extensions handle free-form text through LLM comparison \cite{chen2024usc}, sub-claim decomposition \cite{thirukovalluru2024atomic}, or hallucination detection \cite{manakul2023selfcheckgpt}.
Test-time scaling studies \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys} and reward-free selectors \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty, kim2026reasc, wang2025rankedvoting, oh2026latentsc} all rely on answer-level agreement signals that assume equivalence can be determined via exact match or semantic similarity.
Concurrently, \citet{feng2025optimal} and \citet{wang2025make} adapt self-consistency to difficulty-aware settings; \citet{li2025llms} propose generative self-aggregation for IE but focus on fusion rather than selection.
Our work extends self-consistency to set-valued structured outputs and identifies the correlation-selection gap.

\paragraph{Consistency for structured IE.}
\citet{yao2026consistency} study consistency--accuracy correlations for LLM-based NER/RE under hard-prompting, leaving open whether structural matching improves on surface agreement, whether quality estimation translates to selection, and whether findings generalize across a difficulty gradient---the three questions we address.
Our experiments use fine-tuned models---the dominant deployment paradigm for production NER---where instance degeneracy is most pronounced.
Degeneracy scales with model capability: CoNLL (91\% single-sample F1) exhibits 58\% degeneracy; SciERC (66\%) shows 21\%; WNUT-17 (${\approx}$42\%, macro) shows near-zero (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
This creates an inherent tension between model quality and selection utility that we expect to intensify as models improve.
CoCoA \cite{vashurin2025cocoa} fuses confidence with consistency for QA/summarization but does not address structured extraction; our supervised verifier baseline (logistic regression on all five signals, no oracle gap closure; \S\ref{sec:robustness_main}) suggests that the combination strategy itself is not the bottleneck.
\citet{culotta2004confidence} and \citet{mejer2010confidence} pioneer confidence estimation for structured prediction via CRF marginals and confidence-weighted models; \citet{fomicheva2020unsupervised} systematically apply model-internal signals (MC Dropout, D-Lex) for unsupervised quality estimation in NMT, establishing the paradigm we extend from sequence-level to set-valued structured outputs.
Our evaluation builds on generative IE work \cite{zhou2024uniner, sainz2024gollie, li2023codeie, wadhwa2023revisiting} and constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided, park2024grammar}; recent work highlights hidden costs of constrained generation for log-probability estimation \cite{schall2025hidden} and inference efficiency \cite{yun2025price}.

\paragraph{Uncertainty estimation and calibration.}
Surveys cover confidence estimation \cite{geng2024confidence}, uncertainty quantification \cite{xia2025survey}, and calibration \cite{hobelsberger2025systematic} for LLMs.
Semantic uncertainty \cite{kuhn2023semantic} clusters generations by meaning; P(True) \cite{kadavath2022language} queries model confidence directly; \citet{malinin2021uncertainty} study predictive uncertainty for autoregressive structured prediction.
Our structural signals instead measure agreement over output \textit{structure}, requiring no model modification.
Our selection strategies instantiate MBR decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, deguchi2024centroid} with structural utility functions.
Unlike machine translation where MBR yields consistent gains \cite{freitag2022high}, we find that utility \textit{is} aligned with quality (within-instance SJ--F1 $\rho{=}0.52$) but instance degeneracy eliminates the headroom MBR would otherwise exploit.
\citet{eikema2025structured} find that standard MBR utilities degrade on structured outputs due to bag-of-unit mismatches; our diagnosis is complementary---the bottleneck is not utility misalignment but output concentration driven by model capability (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
\citet{xie2024selfevaluation} show self-evaluation improves selective generation for discrete tasks; our results suggest this does not transfer to structured extraction without learned scoring.
Our quality estimation results connect to selective prediction \cite{kuleshov2015calibrated}: signals with $\rho$ up to 0.45 on CoNLL (0.42 on the primary test bed) and AUROC up to 0.82 can support abstention policies that flag low-quality extractions, providing practical value independent of sample selection.
Conformal prediction constructs prediction sets with coverage guarantees \cite{zhang2025conformal}; while complementary, its set-valued output differs from best-of-$N$ selection.

\paragraph{Best-of-$N$ with learned verifiers.}
\citet{gao2023scaling} establish scaling laws for best-of-$N$ selection with learned reward models, showing that BoN performance scales log-linearly with $N$ but eventually degrades due to reward overoptimization.
Our unsupervised signals face a more fundamental limitation: they cannot rank candidates at all (instance-level signals) or rank them too weakly (LP compression), making the overoptimization regime irrelevant.
Trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, lightman2024verify} and quality-aware decoding \cite{fernandes2022quality} learn per-sample scoring that may bridge this gap; our LoRA-rank ablation (degeneracy 7\% vs.\ 21\%, selection still fails) suggests that verifier training is necessary beyond merely increasing output diversity.
Fine-tuning itself contributes to the problem: \citet{kirk2024understanding} document diversity collapse in RLHF-trained models; our instance degeneracy is an analogous phenomenon in supervised fine-tuning, where stronger models converge to more uniform outputs.
Nucleus sampling \cite{holtzman2020curious} improves diversity in open-ended generation, but our constrained structured outputs limit the diversity that temperature scaling alone can recover.

299	\paragraph{Output diversity quantification.}
300	Table~\ref{tab:diversity} summarizes output diversity across configurations.
301	On SciERC, output diversity is substantial: Qwen produces 43\% unique outputs per instance (mean 3.5 distinct out of $N{=}8$), with per-sample F1 standard deviation of 0.144 and mean pairwise SJ of 0.703.
302	LLaMA shows similar diversity (39\% unique, F1 std 0.11).
303	On CoNLL, diversity collapses: 57\% (Qwen) to 88\% (LLaMA) of instances produce identical outputs across all $N$ samples, reflecting a ceiling effect where single-sample F1 already exceeds 0.90.

329	On the 44\% of Qwen SciERC instances with high diversity (${\geq}4$ unique outputs among 8 samples, $n{=}232$), oracle headroom reaches $+$16.3~pp, yet all consistency-based signals (SJ, FK, EM, VC) select at or below single-sample, and LP---the only per-sample signal---achieves merely $+$0.8~pp.
